title: Decorator
summary: Wrap an object to add behaviour without changing it or subclassing it.

steps.title: Adding behaviour around an object
body: You have an `IDataSource` that reads and writes text. Now you need logging. Later, compression. Sometimes both, sometimes neither.
**Decorator**: a class that implements the same interface *and* wraps another instance of it, adding something before or after delegating.
class FileSource : IDataSource { public string Read() => "data"; }
The caller sees an `IDataSource` and cannot tell. Decorators stack like layers of an onion.

steps.prompt: Decorators stack. What does this print?
code: IText t = new Exclaim(new Upper(new Plain("hi")));
class Plain(string s) : IText { public string Get() => s; }
class Upper(IText inner) : IText { public string Get() => inner.Get().ToUpper(); }
class Exclaim(IText inner) : IText { public string Get() => inner.Get() + "!"; }

steps.prompt: What makes a class a decorator rather than just a wrapper?
options: It implements the **same** interface as the object it wraps, so it can be used anywhere that object can
It inherits from the concrete class it wraps
It uses reflection to intercept calls

steps.prompt: Good job for a decorator, or better kept inside the class?
items: The core formula that computes a price
Validation that is specific to one entity's fields

steps.title: Where you have seen it
body: - `new BufferedStream(new FileStream(...))` and `new GZipStream(stream, ...)` are all `Stream`s
- ASP.NET middleware wraps the next handler
Typical decorator jobs: logging, caching, retry, timing, authorisation, validation. All are **cross-cutting**: they apply to many classes and have nothing to do with the core job.
Overkill check: if the extra behaviour is always on and only applies to one class, put it in that class.

steps.prompt: Arrange the caching decorator so it returns the cached value when it has one, and otherwise asks the inner source and remembers the answer.
You have caching, logging and retry decorators. In which order should you wrap a slow, flaky service so that cache hits skip both the log and the retries?
steps.explain: The outermost decorator runs first. Caching on the outside answers from the cache before the inner layers are reached.

steps.title: A counting decorator
prompt: `IGreeter` and `Greeter` are given. Without changing them, write two decorators:
- `class CountingGreeter(IGreeter inner) : IGreeter` that counts calls in `public int Calls { get; private set; }`
- `class PoliteGreeter(IGreeter inner) : IGreeter` that appends ` Have a nice day.` to whatever the inner greeter says
starter: class Greeter : IGreeter { public string Greet(string name) => $"Hello, {name}."; }
solution: class Greeter : IGreeter { public string Greet(string name) => $"Hello, {name}."; }
public int Calls { get; private set; }
public string Greet(string name) => inner.Greet(name) + " Have a nice day.";
template: Dojo.Eq("polite and counted", "Hello, Ada. Have a nice day.", dojoG.Greet("Ada"));
Dojo.Eq("works the other way round too", "Hello, Cy. Have a nice day.", new CountingGreeter(new PoliteGreeter(new Greeter())).Greet("Cy"));
